definition.en-US: A branch is a separate line of work that starts from the main version of a project, so changes on it do not reach main until you choose to merge them.

analogy.en-US: It is like a sheet of tracing paper laid over a drawing, where you sketch changes that stay separate until you copy them onto the original.

definition.en-US: A commit is a saved checkpoint that records the changes to one or more files, together with a message that says what changed.

analogy.en-US: It is like dating and labelling a photo album page after you have added the pictures to it.

definition.en-US: To push means to send your saved commits and branches from your computer to GitHub.

analogy.en-US: It is like uploading a finished photo album to a shared cloud folder so that the whole family can see it.

definition.en-US: A pull request is a proposal to merge the changes on one branch into another, with a place for people to review and discuss them first.

analogy.en-US: It is like handing your homework to a teacher for marking before it counts toward your grade.

definition.en-US: To merge means to combine the changes on one branch into another branch, usually into main.

analogy.en-US: It is like pouring the water from one glass into a larger jug, so that the contents of both end up in one place.

definition.en-US: The base branch is the branch that a pull request would merge into, such as main.

analogy.en-US: It is like the final copy of a shared essay, into which each suggested paragraph is copied once the teacher approves it.

definition.en-US: An issue is a written note on GitHub that describes a bug, an idea or a request, and that people can discuss.

analogy.en-US: It is like a sticky note on a community board that says what needs fixing, so anyone can add a comment under it.

definition.en-US: A fork is your own copy of another repository on GitHub, which stays connected to the original.

analogy.en-US: It is like copying a recipe into your own cookbook, where you can change it freely while the original book stays the same.

definition.en-US: Open source software is software whose source code is shared so that others may read, use and change it under a license.

analogy.en-US: It is like a community cookbook that anyone may copy and adapt, as long as they follow the rules printed on its first page.
